quantity: Cross-sectional association between long nocturnal sleep and the odds of MCI in community-dwelling Chinese adults (logistic-regression odds ratio). Population-level association from two independent national cohorts (CHARLS 2018, CLAS 2011-12).
contrast: Long sleepers against normal-duration sleepers, with MCI vs no MCI as the outcome. P-891 compares a >=8 h category with a 6-8 h reference. P-773 estimates a per-additional-hour slope within its late-life >=7 h stratum.
finding_a: P-891 (CHARLS 2018, n=7,480, adults 45+, MCI defined by TICS-10 screening): 'Short (<=6 h) and long (>=8 h) sleep durations ... were linked to higher odds of MCI'. The long-sleep odds ratios are stratified by sleep quality: OR 1.88 with poor quality vs 1.33 with good quality, against the 6-8 h reference. The block prints no unstratified long-sleep OR and no confidence interval.
finding_b: P-773 (CLAS, n=2,977, ages 60-96, Petersen amnestic MCI): 'Among those sleeping 7 hours or more in late life, additional sleep showed no significant association with aMCI (OR 0.91, 0.77-1.08, p = 0.283).' The stratum is 1,543 participants (mean 7.68 +/- 0.82 h) with 245 aMCI cases, so it is not a small-sample null.
why_same_quantity: Both are population-level associations of long sleep with MCI odds, not model-performance claims. Both samples are community-dwelling Chinese older adults (P-891 includes adults from 45, and P-773's late-life stratum sits inside P-891's age range). Both use cross-sectional logistic ORs, and all deterministic gates pass (T6, cross_sectional, general, survey_questionnaire, V2). Under the rule for different cohorts, the cohort mismatch can be waived because the claim is about a population association. The operator's own G4 note (2026-09-09) said the intervals are 'formally incompatible' (P-773 upper bound 1.08 vs P-891 1.33/1.88), and the closure mainly cites the MCI definition and the form of the contrast. It does not show that the underlying association differs.
why_incompatible: The point estimates run in opposite directions: long sleep is harmful in P-891 (OR >1 in both quality strata) and slightly protective or null in P-773 (OR 0.91 per hour). P-773's per-hour upper bound of 1.08 sits below the per-hour effect that P-891's >=8 h ORs of 1.33 and 1.88 imply. If P-891 reports a comparable long-sleep contrast with a CI, the two estimates could exclude each other.
concerns: Most likely this stays closed, because the closure does show real differences in quantity. (1) The estimands differ: P-773 gives a per-hour slope inside a >=7 h stratum, while P-891 gives a >=8 h category against a 6-8 h reference, stratified by sleep quality. The 2026-09-14 audit found that P-891's block prints no unstratified long-sleep OR and no CI, so the operator's 'intervals incompatible' remark is unsupported as the records stand. (2) The outcomes differ: TICS-10 screening MCI from age 45 vs clinically defined amnestic MCI at 60-96, with vascular MCI and depression excluded. (3) P-773's own continuous analysis (MoCA) gives the same inverted U, with a late-life optimum of 6.87 h. On the continuous outcome, then, both papers agree that long sleep goes with worse cognition. The apparent disagreement reduces to significance on the dichotomous aMCI limb, which the rule does not count as incompatible. (4) Both papers carry authors_overclaim flags. The pair can be admitted only if the P-891 PDF prints an unstratified long-sleep OR (ideally for age >=60) with a CI that excludes what P-773's interval allows for an equivalent contrast, and P-773 or its supplement gives a matching categorical long-sleep estimate. I checked every other record in the file and none qualifies. Most are spreads between different classifiers. C-228, C-229, C-243 and C-245 differ in intervention or estimand, or are significant-vs-null. C-231 and C-251 are at different disease stages. C-244 compares different methods on non-independent samples. C-230 remains a non-contradiction, though not for the reason recorded: P-632's process-dissociation familiarity also tested recently studied items, so the recency moderator does not settle it. The real grounds are that P-667's only significant familiarity contrast is young vs MCI (older adults vs MCI is not significant) and the two studies measure familiarity differently (process dissociation vs ROC).
population_a: CHARLS 2018 community-dwelling Chinese adults aged 45+, n=7,480
population_b: CLAS 2011-12 community-dwelling Chinese adults aged 60-96, late-life stratum sleeping >=7 h, n=1,543 (245 aMCI)

source: IA-67 (prior KA-22; P-674 is listed among the record's supporting papers)
quantity: Pooled effect of an exercise-only intervention against a non-exercise control on global cognition in older adults with MCI, as a standardised mean difference of change scores from RCTs
contrast: Exercise alone vs non-exercise control (usual care, health education, stretching or placebo activity), global cognition, MCI at baseline
population_a: MCI-at-baseline subgroup of a meta-analysis of 16 long-term (12 months or more) RCTs in non-demented community-dwelling older adults. The MCI subgroup is 3 trials: van Uffelen 2008, Lam 2012 and Lam 2015
population_b: Adults aged 60+ who meet Petersen MCI criteria. 21 RCTs, 1,916 analysed. Exercise-only arms (aerobic, resistance, multicomponent, neuromotor). Combined interventions were excluded
finding_a: P-249 (Reparaz-Escudero 2024, Ageing Res Rev), PDF section 3.10: long-term physical exercise had 'a negligible impact on participants diagnosed with MCI at baseline (SMD = 0.06; 95% CI: -0.10, 0.21)'. Exercise alone across all populations: SMD 0.05 (-0.04 to 0.13). The pooling used HKSJ random effects on change-from-baseline scores. The MCI subgroup figure is in the PDF but not in the summary block.
finding_b: P-674 (Ahn & Kim 2023, Arch Gerontol Geriatr), abstract: 'The mean effects (standardized mean differences) were 0.65 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.39-0.91) for global cognitive function ... in older adults with MCI who received exercise therapy'. DerSimonian-Laird random effects, Hedges' g, I-squared 85%.
why_same_quantity: Both are RCT-only syntheses. Both pool exercise-alone arms, not multidomain packages, against non-exercise controls. The outcome is the same (global cognition, SMD across MMSE/MoCA/ADAS-Cog-type instruments), in the same population class (clinically defined MCI in older adults), with the same metric family (change-score SMD). They even share two trials (Lam 2012, Lam 2015).
why_incompatible: The 95% CIs are disjoint: P-249's MCI upper bound of 0.21 lies below P-674's lower bound of 0.39. The average effect of exercise on global cognition in MCI cannot be both at most 0.21 and at least 0.39. This is not a significant-vs-non-significant difference. Each interval excludes the other's whole range.
concerns: (1) Estimand risk. P-249 admits only trials of 12 months or more, while P-674 measures at the end of mostly 8-24 week programmes. Intervention duration, or the small-study effects that come with short trials, may be a moderator that makes these different estimands ('long-term' vs 'end-of-short-programme' effect). This is the strongest objection. (2) P-249's MCI subgroup has only k=3, dominated by two Hong Kong tai chi trials. (3) P-674 has I-squared 85%, so its prediction interval (about -0.45 to 1.75) contains 0.06. Its sensitivity section also quotes 0.53 against 0.65. (4) Both pool non-interchangeable instruments as unit-free SMDs. That is the defect behind the rejected fourth pair, but here the gap is interval-disjoint, not significance-only. (5) The P-249 summary block should be amended to carry the MCI subgroup estimate before citation.

source: IA-67 (prior KA-22; P-680 is quoted as a holder of the prior and is listed among the record's supporting papers)
quantity: Pooled effect of exercise against a non-exercise control on global cognition in older adults with MCI (standardised difference in means)
contrast: Exercise (aerobic, resistance or multimodal, with no concurrent cognitive task) vs control, global cognition, MCI
population_a: MCI-at-baseline subgroup (3 long-term RCTs) of a synthesis of 16 trials of 12 months or more
population_b: Older adults with MCI (mean age 75.1). 20 studies entered the global-cognition pool. Four amnestic-MCI studies were excluded from the quantitative analysis
finding_a: P-249 PDF section 3.10: MCI at baseline, SMD 0.06 (95% CI -0.10 to 0.21).
finding_b: P-680 (Akalp et al. 2024, Arch Gerontol Geriatr), PDF: 'effect size (ES): 1.165; 0.741 to 1.589 (95% CI; p < 0.001)'. I-squared 88%. Prediction interval -0.747 to 3.077.
why_same_quantity: Both compare exercise arms with non-exercise controls in MCI on global cognition and report a pooled standardised mean difference of change.
why_incompatible: The 95% CIs are disjoint (0.21 vs 0.741). This is independent corroboration of the P-249 vs P-674 gap from a different trial set, since P-680 required studies that also measured blood BDNF/TNF-alpha.
concerns: Weaker than P-249 vs P-674. (1) P-680 standardises by the SD of change scores, which inflates SMDs relative to baseline-SD standardisation, so the metric is not constructed identically. (2) Trial selection is conditioned on reporting blood markers. There is no duration restriction, while P-249 requires 12 months or more. (3) Its prediction interval contains P-249's estimate. (4) It excludes amnestic MCI from the pool, and P-249's MCI trials may be amnestic, so the population subtype may differ. Treat as supporting evidence for the P-249/P-674 candidate, not as a separate headline conflict.

source: IA-27 (prior KA-20, attested 2026-09-27)
quantity: Subfoveal choroidal thickness (OCT) in MCI vs cognitively normal controls, as a standardised group difference
contrast: MCI vs cognitively normal controls, SFCT
population_a: Meta-analysis of OCT studies. MCI choroidal-thickness cell k=4, n=427
population_b: Duke outpatient clinic, 74 MCI (143 eyes) vs 137 controls (248 eyes). Diabetes, glaucoma and retinal pathology excluded
finding_a: P-830 (Ge et al. 2021, Ageing Res Rev), abstract: MCI had lower 'subfoveal choroid (SMD = -0.462, p = 0.020)' than healthy controls. The CI is printed only in Fig. 4. From p=0.020 the normal-approximation CI is about -0.85 to -0.07.
finding_b: P-363 (Robbins et al. 2021, Am J Ophthalmol 223:359), Table 2: SFCT MCI 262.59 +/- 72.88 vs controls 274.12 +/- 98.26 um. Unadjusted difference -10.73 um (95% CI -32.66 to 11.20, p=.338). Adjusted for age, sex and visual acuity: -5.90 um (-27.89 to 16.08, p=.599). Abstract: 'SFCT may not differ among these groups'.
why_same_quantity: Same imaging measure (OCT subfoveal choroidal thickness), same contrast (MCI vs cognitively normal), same population class (clinical MCI in older adults), both expressible as a group mean difference.
why_incompatible: Opposite verdicts (thinning vs no difference). P-363's unadjusted interval, converted with a pooled SD of about 87 um (SMD about -0.12, CI about -0.37 to 0.13), excludes P-830's point estimate of -0.462.
concerns: This probably FAILS H.1 and is included so it is not re-mined. The intervals overlap: P-830's implied CI (-0.85 to -0.07) contains P-363's point estimate, which is the 'different magnitudes with overlapping intervals' exclusion. P-830 does not print its SFCT CI in the text. P-830 cites P-363 (as 'Robbins et al., 2020') in its choroidal-angioarchitecture cell, and whether P-363 also sits inside the k=4 SFCT pool is unknown, so the two may not be independent. P-363's headline estimate is covariate-adjusted, while the pooled SMD is unadjusted. Note also that IA-27 is 'confirmed' as a contradiction of the P-830 prior, but on these numbers it bounds that prior rather than contradicting it.

quantity: How well baseline sulcal width discriminates MCI converters (MCIc/pMCI) from non-converters (MCInc/sMCI) compared with cortical thickness. Both papers extract sulcal width with ENIGMA-Sulci/BrainVISA Morphologist and cortical thickness with FreeSurfer Desikan-Killiany regions.
contrast: sulcal width vs cortical thickness for MCI-to-AD conversion discrimination (MCIc vs MCInc)
finding_a: P-560 (Bologna, n=87, 37 MCI, about 2-year follow-up): sulcal width was the most discriminating feature and outperformed cortical thickness in every contrast. The best single sulcus (right S.T.i.post width) gave AUC 0.907 for MCIc vs MCInc (corrected p=0.001), and no cortical-thickness region differed between MCIc and MCInc.
finding_b: P-198 (ADNI phases 1-2, 721 MCI, two-state Markov transition model with covariates): the cortical-thickness model had AUC 0.78 +/- 0.08 (accuracy 0.75 +/- 0.02) against 0.71 +/- 0.09 for the sulcal-feature model and 0.56 for the no-covariate baseline, so cortical thickness came out ahead.
why_same_quantity: Both papers compare the same two structural MRI measures, built with the same extraction toolchains, on the same prognostic task (telling MCI patients who convert to AD from those who stay stable) in clinical MCI of older adults. They make opposite ordering claims about which measure discriminates better.
why_incompatible: Taken at face value, the orderings point in opposite directions. P-560 finds sulcal width better than thickness, with thickness carrying no significant conversion signal. P-198 ranks thickness above sulcal width, and its thickness model clearly beats a no-covariate baseline.
concerns: Most likely fails the rule, so treat this as a candidate for adjudication, not an admission. (1) P-198's own ordering is not supported by its own statistics: 0.78 +/- 0.08 and 0.71 +/- 0.09 overlap, and no test is reported. The contradiction therefore rests on one side only. (2) This is a performance comparison between different models (P-560: best of 106 single sulci picked in-sample, univariate logistic ROC, leave-one-out; P-198: cross-validated AUCs from a Markov transition model), and the data are different (single-site Bologna 1.5T vs multi-site ADNI). The rule admits a model-performance ordering only on the same task and data, and the dataset-family waiver applies only to population-level associations. (3) P-560's 'thickness not significant' result comes from about 37 MCI patients, an underpowered null that cannot exclude P-198's thickness AUC. P-560's best-feature AUC is also inflated by selecting 1 sulcus from 106 in-sample. (4) Follow-up horizons and conversion definitions differ (about 2 years clinical classification vs transition probabilities). Admit this only if P-198 reports a formal test showing thickness significantly beats sulcal width, or if P-560 reports a thickness AUC whose interval excludes P-198's.
population_a: clinical MCI (MCIc/MCInc), HC and AD, S.Orsola-Malpighi / IRCCS Bologna, Italy, n=87
population_b: 721 MCI from ADNI phases 1-2
source: atoms P-560 ('Sulcal width vs cortical thickness for group discrimination') and P-198 ('MRI-covariate models (sulcal width, cortical thickness) vs baseline no-covariate model'); checked against summaries.md blocks at lines 48173 (P-560) and 9678 (P-198)

quantity: Association of depressive symptoms with prevalent MCI (adjusted logistic-regression odds ratio), community-dwelling Chinese older adults
contrast: Higher vs lower depressive symptoms, odds of prevalent MCI vs normal cognition, fully adjusted cross-sectional model
finding_a: Table 2 of P-878 reports depressive symptom OR 0.956 (95% CI 0.937-0.976), fully adjusted, crude OR 0.940 (0.922-0.957). Read literally, more depressive symptoms mean lower odds of MCI. CHARLS 2015, n=2431.
finding_b: P-644: depressive symptoms (GDS-30 at cut-off 11) OR 1.82 (95% CI 1.20-2.76, p=0.005), fully adjusted, so more depressive symptoms mean higher odds of MCI. Tianjin/Shanghai community sample, n=1394.
population_a: CHARLS 2015 wave, community-dwelling Chinese adults (atom says 45+; the extract's exclusion rule and discussion say 50+), national sample
population_b: Community-dwelling Chinese adults aged 60+, Tianjin and Shanghai
why_same_quantity: Both are cross-sectional studies of community-dwelling Chinese older adults. Both estimate the adjusted odds of prevalent MCI against normal cognition as a function of depressive symptoms, by multivariable logistic regression. Both sit inside the same sarcopenia-depression-MCI bidirectional mediation design. Of the atoms that disagree with P-878 (P-644, P-791, P-785, P-259, P-970, P-1067, P-754), P-644 is the most comparable: same population class, same outcome (prevalent, not incident, MCI), same metric type (OR).
why_incompatible: On the face of the atoms, the directions are opposite and both significant. The two confidence intervals (0.937-0.976 vs 1.20-2.76) sit on opposite sides of 1. That meets the letter of the rule.
concerns: This pair most likely DISSOLVES when P-878 is read. I checked the P-878 extract (pdf_extract_878.txt, Heliyon 10 (2024) e33832). Its own Table 1 shows MORE depression in the MCI group: CESD-10 median 6 vs 5 (p<0.001), and depressive symptoms in 119/439 (27.12%) of MCI vs 310/1992 (15.56%) of NC. Computed from those counts, the crude OR is about 2.02, the same direction and size as P-644's 1.82. The paper's own statistics therefore do not support the opposite direction, which the rule requires. The Results text calls it a 'substantial correlation' and reports a positive total effect (c=0.006) for depression on MCI in the mediation model. Table 2 signs for the other continuous predictors are also inverted against Table 1. Handgrip OR 1.047 per unit, although MCI grip is lower (27.25 vs 31.83). FTSST OR 0.946, although MCI is slower (9.81 vs 9.02 s). This points to reversed outcome/reference coding, or a reporting error, in Table 2. The Results text also misstates Table 1 ('lower depression scores' in MCI). Recommendation: record the pair as a candidate reclassified on reading. Correct the P-878 claim atom/registry value; do not admit this as a genuine contradiction. Secondary non-comparabilities even if the sign were real: CESD-10 scored per point vs GDS-30 dichotomised at 11. MCI defined by an HRS telephone battery (1 SD below age-band norm) vs Petersen criteria with education-stratified MMSE, IADL and CDRS. Different covariate sets. Age floor 50 vs 60. No other pair among the 79 atoms meets the rule. The rejected near-misses were: significance-only or overlapping differences (P-1142 vs P-26; P-989 HR 1.21 (0.88-1.67) vs P-605 HR 1.39 (1.10-1.76); P-670 vs P-26). Underpowered nulls (P-883 n=40 vs P-997). Different population class (P-831 SCD, RR 0.98 (0.75-1.26), vs P-791 general CHARLS older adults, RR 1.45 (1.27-1.65): the intervals barely separate, but SCD is not the same population class). Different measures and populations (P-647 GDS-BDT in MCI vs P-862 GDS-composite in cognitively unimpaired). Different interventions (P-743 vs P-655/P-610).
source: Atoms P-878 and P-644; verified against summaries.md blocks (lines 134496 and 56461) and the P-878 PDF extract, Table 1 and Table 2 (pdf_extract_878.txt in the repo root)

quantity: Crude (unadjusted) sex difference in screen-defined MCI prevalence among community-dwelling older adults
contrast: female vs male prevalence of MCI
finding_a: CHARLS 2020 wave (China, n=4,626 five-wave completers, baseline aged 45+): MCI prevalence females 15.3% vs males 7.7%, p<0.001. MCI defined as CHARLS 31-point global cognition score 1 SD below the age-adjusted normative mean. The contrast is descriptive, reported alongside the paper's prediction model.
finding_b: Toon Health Study (Japan, n=1,094 community-dwelling adults aged 60+, 37.6% men): probable MCI (MoCA-J <26) men 204/411 (49.6%) vs women 211/683 (30.9%), P<0.01 (Table 1 descriptive). Mean MoCA-J was also lower in men (25.2 vs 26.4, P<0.01).
why_same_quantity: Both papers report a population-level descriptive association, not model performance: the crude proportion with screen-defined MCI by sex in community-dwelling Asian older-adult cohorts. Both use a cognitive-screen cut-off rather than a clinical diagnosis, both compare crude proportions with a significance test, and neither adjusts the sex contrast. Under the different-cohort waiver the claim is population-level, and both cohorts sample community-dwelling older adults. Other female-higher atoms were less comparable: P-266 samples middle-aged adults aged 40-60, P-970 is a tertiary-care case-control sample, and P-258 reports an adjusted nomogram predictor with no OR. So P-822 is paired with P-325, the closest female-higher study in design and metric.
why_incompatible: The directions are opposite and each is significant by the study's own test: women about 2x more prevalent in P-325 (p<0.001), men about 1.6x more prevalent in P-822 (P<0.01). Read as one quantity (which sex carries more screen-defined MCI in community older adults), the two cannot both hold.
concerns: This is serious and probably dissolves on adjudication. (1) Different national populations. A crude sex gap in MCI prevalence is a population-specific descriptive, not a universal parameter. In older Chinese cohorts it is strongly driven by the female education deficit, and neither screen is education-corrected here (the P-325 norm is age-adjusted only; MoCA-J <26 has no education point in the extract). So both results can be true of their own populations, which fails the 'both cannot be true' test unless the estimand is framed as a biological sex effect, and neither paper estimates that. (2) Different outcome instruments and cut-offs: a CHARLS composite at -1 SD vs MoCA-J <26. That gives very different base rates (13.7% vs 37.9%). (3) Different age ranges: CHARLS baseline 45+ (about 54+ by 2020) vs Toon 60+. The sex-specific age distributions are not reported. (4) Selection: P-325 keeps only five-wave completers (4,626 of 17,705), and P-822 draws on volunteer health-examination attendees who are 62% women. (5) Neither contrast is adjusted for age, education or other covariates. Both are Table-1 style chi-square comparisons. (6) Neither paper's primary aim is the sex difference, so both are secondary descriptives.
population_a: Chinese community-dwelling middle-aged and older adults, CHARLS national survey (baseline 45+), 2020 wave
population_b: Japanese community-dwelling adults aged 60+, Toon Health Study health-examination cohort, Ehime
source: Atoms P-325 and P-822, checked against summaries.md blocks (Paper 325 lines ~24695+, Paper 822 lines ~105812+, Table 1 values quoted in the P-822 block)

quantity: Cross-sectional association between long self-reported nightly sleep duration and the odds of MCI (vs cognitively normal) in community-dwelling Chinese older adults (logistic OR)
contrast: P-773: each additional hour of late-life sleep among those sleeping 7 h or more (continuous slope within the long-sleep arm, n=1,543, 245 aMCI, mean 7.68 +/- 0.82 h). P-878: sleep of 8 h or more vs the reference category (not printed in the block; implied >4 to <8 h), CHARLS 2015 wave.
finding_a: No association above the 7 h optimum: OR 0.91 per hour (95% CI 0.77-1.08, p=0.283) adjusted for age/sex/education; fully adjusted OR 0.92 (0.76-1.10). Below 7 h each extra hour was protective, OR 0.80 (0.68-0.95). Point estimate on the long-sleep side is below 1.
finding_b: Long sleep associated with higher MCI odds: 8 h or more OR 1.446 (95% CI 1.123-1.861, p=0.004), fully adjusted; U-shaped with 4 h or less OR 1.781 (1.331-2.385).
why_same_quantity: Both measure nightly sleep hours by self-report, both estimate a cross-sectional logistic OR for MCI vs cognitively normal, both sample community-dwelling Chinese adults, and both speak to the long-sleep arm of the duration-MCI curve. The estimand overlaps only partly (see concerns).
why_incompatible: If a linear per-hour slope is converted to the 1.5-2 h gap between an 8 h+ group and a mid-range reference, P-773's interval becomes about 0.59-1.17. That excludes P-878's point estimate of 1.446. The implied ceiling falls further once P-773's protective slope between about 6.5 h and 7 h is counted. On this reading, P-773 is an adequately powered null (245 cases in the long-sleep arm) that sits against a significant long-sleep harm estimate. It meets the rule only through a parameterisation conversion, not through directly comparable estimates.
concerns: (1) Different contrasts: P-773 gives a per-hour slope within the 7 h+ group, while P-878 compares an 8 h+ category against a reference that also contains short sleepers. Comparing them needs a linearity assumption, and the implied intervals border on P-878's lower bound of 1.123 rather than clearly excluding it. (2) Different outcome definitions: P-773 uses a clinical Petersen/Portet aMCI diagnosis with informant corroboration. P-878 uses psychometric age-associated cognitive decline (1 SD below age-band norm on the HRS telephone battery), which covers any MCI. (3) Population restriction: P-773 excluded depressive disorder, vascular MCI and other psychiatric diagnoses. P-878 kept depressed participants (adjusting for CESD-10) and includes ages 45-59. Depression is the main suspected confounder of long sleep, so this restriction may change what is estimated. (4) P-773's own continuous MoCA curve is an inverted U with its optimum at 6.87 h and cognition declining beyond it, the same direction as P-878. The papers agree on cognition score and differ only on aMCI-status odds above 7 h. The authors present the inverted U as the explanation for apparent contradictions in the literature. (5) P-878's reference category is not printed in its summary block (summaries.md line ~134496) and needs checking in the PDF. (6) The third comparable study, P-803 (age 60+, MMSE+IADL MCI, categories of 6-8 h reference / 8-9 / 9-10 / >10 h), found only >10 h significant (OR 2.286, 1.293-4.044). That fits P-773 better than P-878 and suggests the disagreement tracks where the long-sleep cut-point is placed. (7) Both designs are cross-sectional and self-reported. Likely to dissolve on a full reading of both papers. Listed as the only same-quantity opposition in the sleep atoms. All other atom pairs either agree in direction (P-819 vs P-821 on TST and SE; P-261 vs P-492 on latency; P-878, P-891 and P-803 on long sleep), use different quantities or populations (CHF, PD-MCI, iRBD, AD vs MCI), or are descriptive prevalences. P-654's pooled 35.8% vs P-1072's 70.1% dyssomnia figure was rejected: P-1072's figure is a secondary bibliometric citation with no interval, it covers a different construct, and P-654 reports I2=98%, so its pooled CI is not a range for single-study values.
source: summaries.md (repo root): P-773 block at line 78066 (Results, Table 3/4 values), P-878 block at line 134496 (Table 2, L244-245, L285), P-803 block at line 90812 (sleep categories, Figure 1 prose)
population_a: Community-dwelling Chinese adults aged 60-96, China Longitudinal Aging Study baseline 2011-2012, 15 sites / 8 provinces, N=2,977 (505 aMCI, 2,472 normal ageing); dementia, vascular MCI, depression and other psychiatric disorders excluded
population_b: Chinese adults aged 45+, CHARLS 2015 national survey wave, n=2,431; MCI by psychometric age-associated cognitive decline criterion

quantity: Obesity (adiposity category) as a predictor of progression from clinical MCI to all-cause dementia, hazard ratio from a confounder-adjusted time-to-event model in a US EHR cohort
contrast: obese vs non-obese MCI patients, hazard of incident all-cause dementia (ICD-coded). P-1081 reference is normal BMI; P-1151 reference is MCI without obesity
finding_a: From the P-1081 PDF, Table 3A (real training set, multivariable Cox with backward stepwise selection, adjusted for age, race, ethnicity, sex and selected comorbidities: cerebrovascular disease, stroke, MI, hypertension, diabetes, alcohol abuse, sleep apnoea). Obese vs normal BMI: HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.71-0.79). Overweight: HR 0.87 (0.83-0.91). BMI p<0.001. The same result appears on all three synthetic training sets (0.74-0.75). The authors call high BMI 'protective' for 5-year MCI-to-ACD conversion. The summary block says no individual HR was given, but the PDF table does give one.
finding_b: From the P-1151 PDF, Figure 2 and Results 3.2 (1:1 propensity-score matched, 4118 vs 4118, matched on age, sex, race, the other three cardiometabolic diseases, vascular/renal comorbidities and medications). Obesity vs no obesity for all-cause dementia within 10 years: HR 1.05 (95% CI 0.97-1.13), RD -0.12. The result was non-significant in every sensitivity analysis except males, where obesity increased risk: HR 1.13 (1.01-1.26). The authors say: 'obesity was not associated with dementia progression overall, except among males, for which obesity conferred an increased risk.'
population_a: US veterans with an MCI diagnosis, VA Corporate Data Warehouse 1999-2016, about 96% male, median age at MCI 71; 59,782 MCI patients
population_b: Adults aged 50 or older with an MCI diagnosis, TriNetX federated US EHR network, enrolled 2010-2017; obesity cohort mean age 68.5, about 55% female; the male stratum is the closest match to the VA cohort
source: P-1081 PDF (downloads/1. Clinical Assessments, Behavioral and Social Factors/PMID_38545542_DAD2-16-e12572.pdf) Table 3A and Results; P-1151 PDF (downloads/1. Clinical Assessments, Behavioral and Social Factors/PMID_40951936_ALZ-21-e70692.pdf) Figure 2 (page 7, HR read from the rendered figure) and Results 3.2 / Discussion 4.1
why_same_quantity: Both estimate the same thing: the hazard of all-cause dementia among patients already diagnosed with clinical MCI, obese vs not obese. Both use HR from time-to-event models on routine US EHR data. Both code MCI and dementia from ICD codes. Both adjust for or match on the vascular and cardiometabolic comorbidities that could mediate the effect (hypertension, diabetes, cerebrovascular disease, MI/ischaemic heart disease), so the adjustment sets are broadly similar. The population class is the same: clinically diagnosed MCI in US adults aged 50 or older in routine care, not PD-MCI, post-stroke MCI or a diabetes-only sample. The claim is a population-level association, not model performance, so the dataset-family mismatch (VA CDW vs TriNetX) can be waived on the record for that reason. P-1081 is about 96% male, so P-1151's male stratum gives a sex-matched comparison.
why_incompatible: The intervals exclude each other in both comparisons. (1) P-1151's primary estimate is a precise, well-powered null, HR 1.05 (0.97-1.13; 1520 events in the exposed arm). Its lower bound of 0.97 excludes P-1081's HR 0.75 (0.71-0.79), whose upper bound is 0.79. (2) In the sex-matched comparison, P-1151's male stratum is significant in the opposite direction: HR 1.13 (1.01-1.26), increased risk, against P-1081's significant protective HR 0.75. The reference-group difference does not remove the conflict. Recombining P-1081's categories to obese vs non-obese (normal plus overweight) gives an HR between 0.75 and 0.87, which is still well below P-1151's lower bounds of 0.97 overall and 1.01 in males.
concerns: (a) The biggest threat is exposure timing, which may change the estimand. P-1081 measures BMI at the MCI diagnosis. P-1151 requires obesity to be diagnosed at least 5 years before the MCI diagnosis and was explicitly designed to reduce reverse causality: prodromal weight loss lowers BMI at diagnosis. P-1081's own discussion attributes the protective effect to late-life BMI and possible disease-related weight decline. An adjudicator could reasonably decide that current BMI at MCI diagnosis and long-standing pre-MCI obesity are different exposures. If so, this pair fails the same-quantity test the same way the four rejected pairs did. (b) Exposure is ascertained differently: P-1081 uses measured BMI category, with 2.43% mean-imputed. P-1151 uses ICD-10 obesity codes plus BMI as a proxy, and obesity codes under-record and select more severe or clinically managed obesity. (c) The reference groups differ (normal BMI vs non-obese), though the recombination argument above suggests this does not close the gap. (d) The horizons differ: 5-year conversion vs a 10-year window with median 7-year follow-up. (e) The designs differ: stepwise-selected multivariable Cox in a prediction paper vs 1:1 propensity-score matching. (f) The significant opposite direction in P-1151 comes from one male-only sensitivity analysis among many subgroup analyses (a multiplicity risk). The overall comparison is a null against a protective effect, which the rule caps at moderate. (g) Veterans differ from the general EHR population in comorbidity burden and healthcare access. Excluded from pairing: P-319 (OneFlorida+) also calls BMI 'negatively associated' with MCI-to-AD conversion, but only as a SHAP/XGBoost feature direction with no effect estimate or significance, and its endpoint is AD rather than all-cause dementia. It cannot anchor a contradiction and would be a weaker partner than P-1081. The other atoms (P-856 BMI in MCI vs controls, P-728 WHR MCI vs SCD, P-650 midlife central obesity and incident MCI, P-339 CVAI in T2DM, P-958 MCRS) have no opposing atom on the same quantity.

quantity: Effect of choline alfoscerate (choline alphoscerate) use vs non-use / no therapy on conversion from MCI to Alzheimer's disease dementia (relative risk of conversion)
contrast: Choline alfoscerate users vs non-users (P-1112, propensity-matched observational) / choline alphoscerate 1200 mg/day vs no therapy (P-1215's cited randomised study)
finding_a: P-1112 (Pyun et al. 2024, Dement Neurocogn Disord): 3,062 propensity-matched CA-user/non-user pairs, MCI patients aged >60, three Korean hospital OMOP-CDM databases, Cox HR meta-analysed across hospitals. MCI to ADD HR 1.05 (95% CI 0.51-1.59). MCI to all-cause dementia HR 0.93 (0.59-1.26). Null in every subgroup (sex, AChEI use, donepezil use).
finding_b: P-1215 (Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience 2025 narrative review, citing Ponomareva et al. 2024): prospective randomised study of 100 amnesic-type MCI patients 'at high risk of Alzheimer's disease'. After 3 years of choline alphoscerate vs no therapy, AD conversion was 8.2% vs 26.1% and cognitive-deficit progression 12.2% vs 39.1%. P-1215 gives no p-value or CI. The percentages fit about 4/49 vs 12/46, which gives RR about 0.31 (my approximate 95% CI 0.11-0.90). These are my reconstructions, not reported figures.
why_same_quantity: Same exposure (choline alfoscerate vs no use/no therapy), same outcome (conversion from MCI to Alzheimer's disease dementia; P-1112 reports ADD separately from all-cause dementia), same population class (clinical MCI in older adults; the Russian study is the amnestic subset), and both are relative-risk estimates of conversion. The claim is about a population-level drug effect, not model performance, so the different-cohort / dataset-family mismatch can be waived on that basis. The metric is not identical: a hazard ratio against a crude 3-year risk ratio.
why_incompatible: Only the weakest admissible form applies: a reasonably precise null whose interval excludes the other study's point estimate. P-1112's ADD interval (0.51-1.59) and its all-cause interval (0.59-1.26) both exclude the Russian point estimate of about 0.31, a roughly two-thirds cut in conversion. If P-1112 is right, a protective effect that large is implausible in Korean clinical MCI. The two intervals are not mutually exclusive, though: the Russian study's reconstructed CI (about 0.11-0.90) overlaps P-1112's between about 0.51 and 0.90. The directions also differ only as significant-protective vs null. They do not point in opposite significant directions.
concerns: (1) P-1215 is a narrative review. The primary source (Ponomareva et al. 2024) is not in the corpus. The atom is a second-hand citation with no reported statistic, so the review's wording ('suggested', 'may help prevent') is the only evidence of significance. (2) Group sizes and the RR/CI are my arithmetic from the percentages, not reported values. (3) Design: open-label randomised vs no therapy (no placebo, so detection/ascertainment bias is possible) against real-world propensity-matched Cox. (4) Population: amnestic MCI selected for high AD risk (enrichment criteria unknown) against all-comer ICD/CDM-coded MCI over 60. (5) Horizon and metric: fixed 3-year cumulative proportion (RR) against variable-follow-up hazard ratio. (6) Exposure: 1200 mg/day protocol dosing against unspecified real-world dosing and adherence. (7) P-1112's CI is symmetric on the linear HR scale, which suggests linear-scale pooling. Event numbers are described as modest. (8) The overlapping intervals mean this is not an 'intervals exclude each other' contradiction. It needs reading of the Ponomareva primary paper before admission. Pairs I considered and rejected under the rule: SSRI P-1158 vs P-1002 (AD dementia HR against all-cause-dementia risk-difference ATE; class vs individual agents; P-1158 null imprecise, CI 0.61-4.38). ChEI P-1216 vs P-929 (progression HR against 1-year cognitive-change OR with CI 0.20-6.24; same harm-or-null direction, no opposition). Linagliptin P-915 human RCT null vs P-1178 aged-mouse benefit (different species/population class). Levetiracetam P-640 vs P-1121 (DG/CA3 BOLD and memory against entorhinal atrophy; different endpoints, and the doses were not contradicted).

quantity: Association of age (per 1-year increase) with reversion from MCI to normal cognition among people with MCI
contrast: Older vs younger age at MCI classification; reverters vs non-reverters (P-986: incidence rate of reversion; P-711: odds of reversion)
finding_a: GAS/SNAC Swedish population cohort, Petersen-criteria MCI (n=744). Fully adjusted Poisson model with a follow-up offset gives IRR for reversion per year of age 1.02 (95% CI 1.01-1.03), p<0.001. Predicted reversion probability is 0.38 at age 60 and 0.46 at age 70. Under the NP-criteria definition (n=375) the IRR is 1.00 (0.98-1.02), p=0.885. The authors say: 'Opposing most previous work ... older age was associated with reversion.'
finding_b: Meta-analysis, pooled random-effects OR for reversion per year of age 0.94 (95% CI 0.92-0.96), 19 studies, I2=92.5%, P<0.001. Younger age goes with reversion.
population_a: Swedish general-population older adults aged 60-102 with Petersen-criteria MCI (Good Aging in Skane)
population_b: People with MCI pooled from 19 community- and hospital-based studies (48-study review, 31,876 subjects)
why_same_quantity: Same exposure (age in years, continuous), same outcome (reversion from MCI to normal cognition among people diagnosed with MCI), same older-adult clinical-MCI population class. Both report a ratio per year of age.
why_incompatible: The two directions are opposite and both significant. P-986's interval (1.01-1.03) lies wholly above 1 and P-711's (0.92-0.96) lies wholly below 1, so the intervals exclude each other.
concerns: The pair is not independent. P-711 Table 1 lists Overton 2023 (the P-986 paper, n=744) among the studies contributing an age estimate, and Overton 2019 from the same GAS cohort is also in the pool. So P-986 is a heterogeneity outlier inside P-711's own pool rather than an outside refutation. With I2 of 92.5% and no prediction interval, a random-effects mean below 1 fits a cohort-specific estimate above 1, and an adjudicator may reasonably call this heterogeneity, not contradiction. The metric types differ (IRR vs OR). The adjustment sets differ: P-986 adjusts for number of impaired domains, BMI, alcohol, education, cohabitation, depression and others, while P-711 does not say whether crude or adjusted ORs were pooled. P-986's own NP-criteria model is null, so the positive age effect depends on the MCI definition used. The P-986 authors attribute the finding to selective attendance (cognitively healthy older adults are more likely to return for follow-up), which is an attrition artefact rather than a biological claim. An independent crude corroboration of the P-711 direction exists in P-671 (NCGG-SGS, Japan): reverters were younger than maintainers (69.6 vs 72.3 years, ANOVA P<0.01). That comparison is unadjusted, so it was not paired.

P-711 Table 3 row 'Age(y) 19 0.94 (0.92-0.96) 92.5% <0.001' and the Table 1 row for Overton 2023, in pdf_extract_711.txt. Neither age result appears in the supplied atom list; both come from the full texts.

quantity: Pooled proportion of people with MCI recruited in clinical/hospital settings who revert to normal cognition
contrast: Random-effects pooled reversion proportion, clinical-based (P-1127) / hospital-based (P-711) study subgroup
finding_a: Clinical-based studies: reversion 8.7% (95% CI 5.9-11.6%), I2=89.9%, 14 studies. Eligibility: follow-up of at least 3 years, at least 50 participants, established criteria; ADNI and etiology-predetermined cohorts excluded (89 studies, mean follow-up 5.2 years).
finding_b: Hospital-based studies: reversion 20% (95% CI 14-27%), I2=98.4%, 14 studies. Eligibility: any follow-up length (includes 12-month studies); case-control, cross-sectional and cohort designs admitted.
population_a: People with MCI in clinical-setting cohorts, international
population_b: People with MCI in hospital-recruited studies, international
why_same_quantity: Both are random-effects pooled estimates of the same descriptive prognosis quantity: the proportion of clinically recruited MCI patients who revert to normal cognition. Both are meta-analyses of the same literature, and the 'clinical' and 'hospital' setting labels mean the same thing.
why_incompatible: The 95% intervals do not overlap: P-1127's upper bound is 11.6% and P-711's lower bound is 14%.
concerns: This may well fail as the same quantity. The follow-up horizon differs by design: P-1127 requires at least 3 years, while P-711 is unrestricted and includes 12-month studies. Horizon is part of what a reversion proportion estimates, and the rule excludes different horizons. P-1127 scores reversion as one of three end-of-follow-up outcomes and says reversion is probably underestimated where studies only split converters from non-converters. P-711 admits ADNI-type and non-cohort designs. With I2 of 90-98% and no prediction intervals, each pooled mean depends heavily on its own study mix, and the overlap between the two study sets is unknown. The directions agree: both find higher reversion in community/population settings, and those estimates overlap (P-1127 28.2% [17.9-38.5] vs P-711 36% [30-42]). So this is a magnitude disagreement in one setting, not a directional one. P-711 never formally tested its setting subgroups.

quantity: Resting-state ALFF in right posterior inferior temporal cortex (ITG / BA37-BA20 border): MCI vs healthy controls
contrast: MCI vs HC, cross-sectional voxelwise group difference in resting-state ALFF
finding_a: ALE meta-analysis (39 DMN rs-fMRI studies; the ALFF/fALFF-increase analysis rests on n=75 subjects and 14 foci). Convergent INCREASE in bilateral fusiform, with the right peak at MNI (51,-60,-12) BA37 in a 12,656 mm3 cluster that also has a declive peak at (39,-69,-9). The extract states no FWE or cluster threshold.
finding_b: Primary 3T rs-fMRI study, 30 MCI (age 55+) vs 30 matched HC, two-sample t-test, FDR p<0.05 (baseline contrast inside a moxibustion trial). ALFF DECREASED in right ITG, peak MNI (60,-45,-12) BA20, 107 voxels, T=-3.68.
population_a: MCI vs HC pooled across ALE studies (running head says aMCI)
population_b: Clinical MCI, Guangxi, China, single site
why_same_quantity: Both are resting-state ALFF contrasts of MCI vs HC in the same hemisphere and region, in the same population class (clinical MCI in older adults). No seed is involved, so the estimand is ALFF at a location. At x=51 the P-517 peak lies lateral to the fusiform and would probably carry the right ITG label in AAL, the atlas P-529 used. This is not yet checked. The two peaks are 17.5 mm apart, which may fall inside a 12,656 mm3 ALE cluster.
why_incompatible: If P-529's peak lies inside P-517's cluster, one region carries a convergent significant increase and an FDR-significant decrease in ALFF for the same contrast. Both cannot hold for that tissue.
concerns: (1) Spatial: the peaks are 17.5 mm apart and the papers name different gyri. It is not shown that they are the same voxels. Overlay P-517 Fig. 2 or the cluster extent on (60,-45,-12) before admitting. (2) ALE convergence is not a pooled effect estimate. It does not rule out single studies that report decreases. (3) P-517's increase analysis is thin: 14 foci from 75 subjects, probably 2 or 3 experiments, well below the roughly 17 experiments recommended for stable ALE. No correction scheme is reported, ALFF and fALFF are pooled, and study selection was restricted to DMN analyses. (4) P-529 is one site with 30 vs 30. (5) P-528, another ALE, reports DECREASED ALFF at right posterior MTG (60,-42,0), 12 mm from P-529's peak and in agreement with it, so P-517 is the outlier. Rejected on the same review: P-513 vs P-528 on 'left STG ALFF'. Their peaks are (-56,8,0) and (-54,-54,28), 62 mm apart, so these are different quantities.
