quantity: Resting-state DMN (PCC-core) seed-based functional connectivity with medial prefrontal cortex: MCI vs healthy controls
contrast: MCI/aMCI vs HC, cross-sectional group difference in DMN seed-based FC to medial PFC
finding_a: ALE meta-analysis: 27 FC studies among 39 total; the increased-FC analysis covers n=604 subjects and 85 foci. Convergent INCREASE in DMN FC at right medial frontal gyrus MNI (4,58,-14) BA10 and left 'anterior cingulate' (-6,56,-12) BA10, together one 848 mm3 cluster. The authors read this as compensation for decreased PCC connectivity. No threshold is stated in the extract.
finding_b: aMCI (n=40) vs HC (n=38), PCC seed at MNI (-5,-49,40), radius 10 mm, AlphaSim p<0.01. Four-group ANOVA eta2 0.085-0.141. Post hoc tests show PCC-seeded FC to bilateral medial superior frontal gyrus significantly DECREASED in aMCI vs HC, and also in the RGD and RGD-aMCI groups.
population_a: MCI vs HC pooled across ALE studies
population_b: Older Han Chinese amnestic MCI without depression vs HC, Nanjing Brain Hospital
why_same_quantity: Both are resting-state DMN seed-based FC to medial prefrontal cortex, MCI vs HC, in clinical (amnestic) MCI in older adults. PCC is the canonical DMN seed. P-517 frames its mPFC increase against decreased PCC connectivity, which suggests PCC-seeded foci feed that cluster.
why_incompatible: The meta-analysis says anterior-DMN (medial PFC) connectivity is INCREASED in MCI. The primary study says PCC-to-medial-PFC connectivity is significantly DECREASED in aMCI. These are opposite directions for anterior-posterior DMN coupling.
concerns: This is likely to fail the same-estimand test. (1) P-517's ALE pools foci from many different seeds and from ICA studies, so what it estimates is where altered DMN FC sits, not the PCC-mPFC edge itself. (2) P-517's cluster is ventromedial (z=-14, BA10). P-774's M-SFG coordinates appear only in supplementary Tables S3/S4, and medial SFG is usually dorsomedial, so the two may be different subregions. (3) The P-517 cluster is tiny (848 mm3) and the ALE threshold is unreported. ALE gives convergence, not a pooled effect. (4) P-774's ROIs come from a four-group ANOVA with an aMCI subgroup and AlphaSim correction. (5) P-1103 (MCI vs HC, HCP-DMN mPFC seed) also finds DECREASED FC to left medial frontal gyrus at (-4,40,-12), T=4.61. That is 16 mm from P-517's peak and supports P-774's direction, but with a different seed. It was not paired separately because P-517 stands alone against both. (6) P-517 and P-774 come from the same institution (Affiliated Brain Hospital of Nanjing Medical University). No overlap in subjects has been established.
source: downloads/5. Neuroimaging and Neurophysiological Biomarkers/PMID_34675797_fnagi-13-708687.pdf (Table 2, Discussion); downloads/1. Clinical Assessments, Behavioral and Social Factors/1-s2.0-S104161022403182X-main.pdf (Results, Fig. 2)

quantity: Plasma phenylalanine level (univariate group difference, direction of the MCI/control ratio)
contrast: MCI vs cognitively normal older controls
finding_a: Plasma 1H NMR, Mann-Whitney U with Benjamini-Krieger-Yekutieli FDR (Q=1%, significance at FDR-corrected p<0.05): phenylalanine significantly ELEVATED in MCI (n=16) vs cognitively healthy controls (n=48) (Results 3.2: 'In MCI vs. controls, phenylalanine, tyramine, glutamate, n(CH3) lipoproteins, and glutamine concentrations were elevated'). Phenylalanine was also the top plasma VIP contributor, and the Discussion restates 'The MCI group had elevated concentrations of phenylalanine ... compared to controls'.
finding_b: Plasma targeted UHPLC-MS/MS MRM (H650 panel with standards): phenylalanine significantly DECREASED in MCI, FC(MCI/CON)=0.90, VIP 2.30, FDR<0.01 (Table 3; 124 MCI vs 47 controls). This sits within a coherent decrease of essential and branched-chain amino acids (valine, leucine, isoleucine, methionine, tryptophan).
population_a: Ethnically mixed older adults aged 65+ from UERJ clinics (Rio de Janeiro, Brazil); MCI clinically diagnosed by neurologists/geriatricians using NIA-AA 2011 (Albert) criteria; cancer, diabetes, thyroid disease, vascular lesions and uncontrolled hypertension excluded; non-fasting morning samples.
population_b: Rural community older adults from 17 Jimo-district villages (Qingdao, China); MCI defined by MoCA-Beijing <26 (education-corrected), controls >=26; comorbidities recorded but not excluded; 12-h fasting samples, plasma separated immediately.
why_same_quantity: Same analyte (phenylalanine), same matrix (plasma), same comparison (MCI vs cognitively normal older adults), same kind of estimate (unadjusted univariate group difference and its direction), and a population-level association claim, not model performance. Both samples are older adults with MCI of no specific aetiology (not PD-MCI, post-stroke or diabetes-defined), so the cohort difference falls under the rule's allowance for two cohorts drawn from the same population class. Adjustment does not separate them either, since both estimates are unadjusted.
why_incompatible: Each paper's own FDR-corrected univariate test supports the opposite direction: significantly higher in MCI (P-1220) vs significantly lower in MCI (P-1396: FC 0.90, FDR<0.01). Plasma phenylalanine cannot be both significantly raised and significantly lowered in MCI relative to cognitively normal older adults. This is not a significant-vs-null or magnitude-only difference.
concerns: (1) Assay: P-1220 uses relative NMR bucket intensities (0.02 ppm bins, Pareto-scaled). Its discriminating phenylalanine bucket is 3.28 ppm (beta-CH2), which overlaps glucose/betaine/TMAO signals, so the assignment is less secure than P-1396's absolute MRM with standards. (2) P-1220 is small (16 MCI) and non-fasting, with no covariate adjustment. (3) P-1396's MCI is a MoCA screen-positive label, not a clinical diagnosis, and its FC is unadjusted with diabetes and other comorbidities retained. P-1220 excluded those comorbidities, so the populations differ in comorbidity burden and diet (urban Brazil vs rural north China). (4) P-1293 (Hirosaki aMCI, EDTA plasma, Biocrates) says 'most amino acids were significantly decreased in aMCI', but its per-amino-acid directions are shown only in Fig. 3g and could not be read from the text, so whether it sides with P-1396 on phenylalanine is unverified. (5) The supplied P-1220 atoms are unreliable: the valine atom ('increased progressively control<MCI<AD') contradicts the paper, where plasma valine was REDUCED in MCI and the rise was in urine/AD. P-1220's atoms need re-extraction before any ledger record is written.
source: P-1220 finding read directly from the PDF (Results 3.2 plasma paragraph, Fig. 1 legend, first Discussion paragraph); it is not among the supplied atoms. P-1396 finding from the PDF Table 3 (consistent with the supplied P-1396 atom on essential amino acids).

quantity: Adjusted per-year effect of baseline age on the rate of reversion from MCI to normal (or sub-MCI) cognition in older adults with MCI, expressed as a rate ratio per year of age
contrast: Older vs younger age (per year) as a predictor of reversion rate among people with MCI at baseline
finding_a: P-217 (Qin et al., Neurology 2023;100:e297; NACC UDS, 6,651 participants with consensus-diagnosed MCI at entry, 24,220 observations, 3-state continuous-time multistate Markov model). Table 1, bidirectional-transition models: age HR for the MCI -> <MCI (reversion) transition = 0.977 (0.972-0.983) Model 1, 0.976 (0.971-0.981) Model 2, 0.981 (0.976-0.987) Model 3. Text: 'Younger age, lower education level, higher independence level, APOE e4 noncarriers status, higher MMSE scores, and lower CDR and FAQ scores were protective factors for reversion.' Older age lowers the reversion rate, and this holds under all three adjustment sets.
finding_b: P-986 (Overton et al., J Alzheimers Dis 2023;91:585; Good Aging in Skane population cohort, Sweden). Petersen-criteria MCI n=744 (323 reverted, median follow-up 7.0 y). Multivariable Poisson model with a follow-up offset and robust variance, Table 4: Age (y) IRR 1.02 (1.01-1.03), p<0.001. Predicted probability of reversion 0.38 (0.33-0.42) at age 60 vs 0.46 (0.42-0.50) at age 70. Abstract/Discussion: 'older age ... had a higher likelihood of reverting to normal'. Under the NP criteria (n=375) the estimate is IRR 1.00 (0.98-1.02), p=0.885.
why_same_quantity: Same exposure: baseline age in years, entered continuously. Same outcome: a transition from MCI to a non-MCI cognitive state, modelled as a rate. P-217 uses a Markov transition intensity; P-986 uses a Poisson incidence rate with a person-time offset. Same metric family: an adjusted rate ratio per year of age. Same population class: older adults with MCI at baseline, followed for many years in a longitudinal cohort. Each adjustment set includes a severity proxy (P-217 M1: sex, education, marital status, living situation, independence, BMI; P-986: impaired-domain count, education, sex, BMI, depression, CVD, lifestyle). Neither set changes what the age term estimates. Validation tier does not apply (association studies). Task: prognosis/transition. Modality family: clinical/neuropsychological. Dataset family differs (NACC vs GAS). Waiver reason: this is a population-level association, and both cohorts sample older adults with MCI.
why_incompatible: The directions are opposite and each is supported by the study's own statistics. P-217's rate ratio is below 1 with the whole CI below 1 (upper bound 0.983-0.987 across three models). P-986's is above 1 with the whole CI above 1 (lower bound 1.01). The intervals do not overlap, so both cannot be true of the same per-year age effect on reversion rate.
concerns: (1) P-986's result depends on the criteria it uses. It is null under P-986's own NP criteria (IRR 1.00), and the descriptive ages hardly differ: Petersen reverters 68.2 vs stable 68.5 y; NP reverters 66.8 vs stable 69.3 y. So the positive IRR appears only in the adjusted rate model. (2) P-986 names the direction as unusual and gives its own moderator: 'Opposing most previous work ... older age was associated with reversion. This probably reflects a study design feature where healthy individuals are more prone to attend follow-up examinations'. This is selective attendance, a candidate moderator that remains open, not a dissolution. (3) Setting and ascertainment differ. NACC ADC participants are diagnosed by clinical consensus. GAS is a random population sample classified actuarially, with cut-offs corrected for age, sex and education. P-711 shows setting moderates reversion prevalence (community 36% vs hospital 20%), though not specifically the age effect. (4) The outcome states differ. P-217's <MCI merges normal cognition with 'impaired but not MCI'; P-986 requires a cognitively normal reverter who meets the full criteria. (5) Bridging context favours P-217's direction. P-711's pooled age OR is 0.94 (0.92-0.96) over 19 studies, and that pool includes P-986 (Overton 2023 is listed in P-711 Table 1), so P-711 is not an independent third arm. P-671 (Japan) also runs in P-217's direction. A reader could therefore judge this partially_resolved or unresolved rather than genuine. Both papers' PDFs were read for the numbers quoted.
population_a: US NACC Alzheimer's Disease Center participants with consensus-diagnosed MCI at entry (2005-2021), >=2 visits
population_b: Swedish population-based cohort (GAS/SNAC, random sample 60+), MCI classified retrospectively by Petersen (primary) and modified NP criteria; mean age at first MCI 68
source: VF-33

quantity: Adjusted per-year effect of baseline age on MCI reversion to normal cognition in community-dwelling older adults with MCI
contrast: Older vs younger age (per year) as a predictor of reverting to normal cognition
finding_a: P-671 (Katayama et al. 2021, NCGG-SGS, Japan; 769 community-dwelling older adults with MCI, 4-year follow-up: 256 reverters, 395 maintainers, 118 converters). Adjusted multinomial logistic regression (Table 5; converters are the implicit reference). Age (years): reverters OR 0.79 (0.75-0.84), maintainers OR 0.88 (0.85-0.93), both p<0.01. Baseline mean age: reverters 69.6, maintainers 72.3, converters 76.4 y. Older age is associated with lower odds of reversion.
finding_b: P-986 (GAS/SNAC Sweden, Petersen-criteria MCI n=744): Poisson IRR for age (y) 1.02 (1.01-1.03), p<0.001. Older age is associated with a higher reversion rate. The NP-criteria estimate is 1.00 (0.98-1.02).
why_same_quantity: Same exposure (baseline age, continuous, per year), the same outcome class (MCI reverting to normal cognition), and the same population class. Both are community-dwelling older adults with MCI followed in population cohorts, which is a cleaner population match than P-217 vs P-986. Dataset family differs (NCGG-SGS vs GAS). Waiver reason: a population-level association in community-dwelling older adults with MCI.
why_incompatible: Opposite signs, each with a CI excluding 1: 0.79 (0.75-0.84) vs 1.02 (1.01-1.03).
concerns: The estimands are not identical. P-671's reference category is converters, so its age OR contrasts reversion with conversion, not reversion with remaining MCI. The reversion-vs-maintenance contrast is only implied: the reverter and maintainer ORs have non-overlapping CIs, with a ratio of about 0.90 per year, but the paper reports no CI for it. P-671 states only that 'reverters and maintainers were significantly younger at the first wave than converters'. Other differences: OR from a two-wave design vs an IRR from a multi-wave person-time model. P-671's estimates come from an imputed sample (complete-case reversion 52.3% vs 33.3% imputed). P-986's criteria-dependence and its own selective-attendance explanation also apply. Both papers sit in P-711's age pool, which runs in P-671's direction. P-671 is listed among VF-33's rejected supporters; P-986 is a supporter.
population_a: Japanese community-dwelling older adults with MCI (NCGG-SGS), mean age 72.1
population_b: Swedish population-based cohort (GAS/SNAC), Petersen/NP-criteria MCI
source: VF-33

quantity: Association of years of education with MCI reversion to normal / sub-MCI cognition
contrast: Higher vs lower education as a predictor of reversion among people with MCI
finding_a: P-217 (NACC, 6,651 MCI; multistate Markov). Education (per year) HR for MCI -> <MCI: Model 1 0.993 (0.978-1.009), Model 2 0.996 (0.980-1.012), Model 3 0.978 (0.962-0.995). Model 3 adds MMSE, CDR, FAQ, GDS and NPI-Q. Text lists 'lower education level' among the factors favouring reversion.
finding_b: P-711 (meta-analysis, 48 studies). Education (low to high) pooled OR for reversion 1.02 (1.01-1.04), 18 studies, I2 41.9%: higher education favours reversion. P-957 and P-1160 report the same direction in single cohorts.
why_same_quantity: Same exposure (educational attainment), the same outcome (reversion from MCI) and the same population class (older adults with MCI). Both are ledger-linked: IA-77 lists P-217 and P-711 together among its supporting papers. The metric differs: a per-year HR vs a pooled OR over mixed education codings.
why_incompatible: In P-217 Model 3 the CI lies wholly below 1 (upper 0.995); P-711's pooled CI lies wholly above 1 (lower 1.01). The directions are opposite.
concerns: P-217's education effect appears only in Model 3, which conditions on current cognitive and functional scores. That changes the estimand to education net of current cognitive level, a plausible cognitive-reserve artefact. Models 1-2 are null and include P-711's direction within their CIs. A pooled OR over heterogeneous education codings is not a per-year HR. Whether P-217 (Qin 2023) sits inside P-711's pool is unchecked. Most likely outcome: documented_incommensurability or false_positive. Listed because the ledger places both papers in the same IA record.
population_a: US NACC ADC participants with MCI at entry
population_b: 48 pooled MCI cohorts across community and hospital settings, 16 countries
source: IA-77

quantity: Relative discrimination (C-index) of Random Survival Forest vs Cox proportional hazards for time to MCI-to-AD progression
contrast: RSF vs CoxPH ordering on the MCI-to-AD survival task
finding_a: P-309 (Guan 2025, NACC UDS 3.0, n=3,674 MCI, one 7:3 split, 13 clinical/neuropsychological/demographic/APOE predictors, no imaging): validation C-index Cox 0.797 (0.798 without APOE e4) vs RSF 0.781 vs XGBoost 0.781. Authors conclude the ML models were 'not better than' Cox. No CI or test is given for the differences.
finding_b: P-344 (Jahani 2025, BMC Med Res Methodol; ADNI n=902, 14 features including FDG-PET, four MRI volumes, APOE e4 and cognitive tests): RSF C-index 0.878 vs CoxPH 0.863 (Weibull 0.862, CoxEN 0.860, GBSA 0.803). Conclusion: RSF outperformed classical survival models.
why_same_quantity: Same two methods, the same task (time to MCI-to-AD progression) and the same metric (C-index). KA-15 cites P-344 as holding the 'ML survival > Cox' prior, and IA-16 presents P-309 as invalidating it, so the orderings are opposite.
why_incompatible: The ordering claims are opposite, but neither study tests the difference (gaps of about 0.015-0.016 C-index), so the results are not shown to exclude each other.
concerns: The data and predictor sets differ (NACC clinical-only vs ADNI with imaging). Precedent C-232 (different predictor sets across cohorts) and the rule's carve-out, which admits ordering claims only on the same task and data, both apply. Neither paper reports a CI for the performance gap. Expected outcome: documented_incommensurability. Listed because the registry pairs these two studies as prior-holder vs invalidator.
population_a: NACC MCI participants, US ADCs
population_b: ADNI MCI participants
source: IA-16

quantity: Baseline FUNSAT task completion time, compared between participants who later mastered all six tasks and those who did not (MCI + NC, remote FUNSAT trial NCT04677944)
contrast: eventual non-graduates (failure to master all six skills) vs graduates, measured at the untrained baseline assessment
finding_a: P-1174 (conference abstract, n=164: 72 NC + 92 MCI): 'Failure to graduate was associated with more baseline errors on all tasks but not longer completion times'. No statistic or interval is given for the completion-time null.
finding_b: P-783 (full paper, same n=164, Table 2, graduates n=129 vs non-graduates n=35): baseline completion times were significantly longer in non-graduates on all three tasks. Ticket 999 vs 1448, t=4.73, p<0.001, d=1.02; ATM t=5.86, d=1.28; medication management t=3.85, d=0.84. Mann-Whitney confirmation all p<.001.
why_same_quantity: Same trial, same software-logged baseline completion time, same outcome (graduation/mastery status), same mixed MCI+NC population, same sample size (72 NC + 92 MCI), and an overlapping author group (Harvey, Kallestrup, Czaja, Dowell-Esquivel). Read literally, P-1174's sentence is a between-group (bivariate) claim, the same comparison P-783 tabulates.
why_incompatible: Read literally, both cannot be true of the same 164 participants. One report has a d of about 1 at p<0.001 on all three tasks; the other says there was no association with longer completion time.
concerns: This is very likely NOT a genuine contradiction. P-1174 and P-783 report the same analysis of the same cohort (P-1174 looks like the conference-abstract version: F=41.40 and 'first 15 minutes' match P-783's own abstract). They are not two studies. P-783's summary block records that P-783's own abstract makes the identical 'no longer completion times' claim, and that its Table 2 and results prose refute it. What holds is multivariate: completion time did not enter the stepwise discriminant function once baseline errors were in it (Ticket-time approximate F=0.01/0.00). So the P-1174 null is a conditional non-entry (adjusted for errors) squeezed into a bivariate null. That is an adjustment that changes what is estimated, and the pair dissolves once both documents are read. P-1174 gives no estimate or interval, so its null is not a precise powered null either. Recommended handling: log it as a reporting inconsistency within one study (and consider treating P-1174 as a companion or duplicate report of P-783/P-653, the same FUNSAT trial). Do not admit it as a genuine contradiction. Surfaced only because the atoms conflict on their face.
population_a: NC and MCI adults in remote computerized FUNSAT skills training (72 NC + 92 MCI)
population_b: MCI and NC participants, FUNSAT trial NCT04677944 (72 NC + 92 MCI)
source: summaries.md Paper 1174 (outcomes field); summaries.md Paper 783 (Table 2 transcription and reporting-defects section, which flags the abstract/table contradiction)

quantity: Effect of DHA supplementation vs placebo on global cognitive function in older adults with MCI (RCT, between-arm change)
contrast: DHA arm vs placebo arm, change in a global cognitive score over follow-up
finding_a: P-740 (Taiwan multisite RCT, n=163, DHA 0.7 g/d for 24 months): the linear mixed-effects model gives a significant negative coefficient for MMSE change against placebo in the DHA arm (beta -0.34, SE 0.14, p=0.02), and in the EPA and EPA+DHA arms as well. The same paper's prespecified adjusted 24-month change comparison for MMSE is null (p=0.11), as are ADAS-cog, ADCS-ADL, QOL and GDS.
finding_b: P-649 (Tianjin single-centre RCT, n=280, DHA 800 mg/d for 12 months): the DHA arm improved full-scale IQ against placebo (beta 0.135, 95% CI 0.034-0.235, square-root-transformed simple WAIS-RC scores), with significant gains in verbal and performance IQ too.
why_same_quantity: Both are double-blind placebo-controlled RCTs of algal/fish-oil DHA at similar daily doses (0.7 vs 0.8 g/d) in older Chinese-speaking adults, each reporting a between-arm treatment effect on a global cognitive outcome from a linear mixed model. The estimand is the same in intent only (the causal effect of DHA vs placebo on global cognition), and even that holds only loosely: the cognitive instrument and the population mix are not the same.
why_incompatible: The directions are opposite and each is significant by the study's own mixed-model statistics: DHA significantly lowered MMSE relative to placebo in P-740 and significantly raised full-scale IQ relative to placebo in P-649. Both cannot be true of one quantity 'DHA effect on global cognition in MCI'. They could both be true if the two outcomes, horizons or populations are actually different quantities, and the concerns below suggest they probably are.
concerns: Under the H.1 rule this probably fails, on three separate points. (1) Different instrument and metric: P-740 is raw MMSE change (0-30 screening scale, lower is worse); P-649 is a beta on square-root-transformed WAIS-RC full-scale IQ. Different instruments are a same-quantity failure (compare the admitted pair that failed on different instruments). (2) Different population class: P-740 mixes 93 amnestic MCI (CDR 0.5) with 70 mild-to-moderate AD (CDR 1-2, DSM-IV-TR), about 43% dementia, drawn from male-predominant veterans' retirement centres; P-649 is community-dwelling MCI only (DSM-IV criteria, GDS 2-3). (3) Different horizon: 24 vs 12 months. Also, P-740's negative MMSE coefficient is a secondary mixed-model result that its own prespecified adjusted 24-month change test does not support (p=0.11), and its exposure manipulation check failed: RBC DHA fell in the supplemented arms and the between-arm fatty-acid change was null (p=0.95), so the harm signal cannot be separated from non-delivery. P-649's effects are small, on a transformed scale, from a single centre, with supplements supplied by a commercial manufacturer. P-740 may also be one of the RCTs pooled in P-151's omega-3 network meta-analysis, which found no pooled effect (SMD 0.39, 95% CrI -0.42 to 1.19). That interval includes both directions, so P-151 neither contradicts nor resolves this pair. Expected disposition at adjudication: not genuine (a different instrument, population class and horizon). It is proposed only because it is the only pair in this topic with opposite significant directions for the same intervention against placebo. No other pair qualifies. P-151's vitamin B complex null vs P-679's folic acid benefit uses different interventions and has overlapping intervals (0.79-0.90). P-744's ketogenic-diet null vs P-394/P-649's MCT benefit pits an imprecise narrative-review null against a different intervention (diet vs supplement). The remaining nulls (P-875 GSPE, P-724 QGP, P-490 OM3FLAV, P-1262 kMCT markers) have no same-intervention counterpart.
population_a: 163 Taiwanese older adults aged 65-94 (93 amnestic MCI CDR 0.5 + 70 mild-to-moderate AD), veterans' retirement centres and one medical centre, male-predominant
population_b: 280 community-dwelling Chinese adults aged 65+ with MCI, Binhai New District, Tianjin
source: summaries.md blocks for Paper 740 (line 70059) and Paper 649 (line 56971), read beyond the atoms to check instrument, dose, population and the P-740 primary-vs-mixed-model discrepancy

quantity: Serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) concentration
contrast: MCI vs cognitively unimpaired controls (cross-sectional group comparison)
finding_a: Serum IL-6 significantly LOWER in MCI than non-impaired controls (NIC): NIC 42.8 vs MCI 3.1 pg/mL, p<0.001 (n=107: 32 MCI due to AD, 45 NIC, 30 serum-only HC; Russia/US samples, MSD/ELISA immunoassay)
finding_b: Serum IL-6 significantly HIGHER (highest) in MCI than in HC and AD, P=0.013 (n=157 community-dwelling adults, Hebei China: 97 HC, 44 MCI, 16 AD; fasting serum ELISA)
population_a: MCI due to AD vs osteoarthritis non-impaired controls, Russia
population_b: Community MCI vs healthy controls, China
why_same_quantity: Same marker (IL-6), same matrix (serum), same assay class (immunoassay), same metric type (group difference in concentration), and both code the comparison as MCI vs cognitively unimpaired controls in older-adult clinical/community MCI. It is a population-level association, so a cross-cohort comparison can be admitted if the control populations belong to the same class.
why_incompatible: At atom level the two directions are opposite and both significant for serum IL-6 in MCI vs cognitively unimpaired controls: lower in MCI (p<0.001) against higher in MCI (P=0.013). Both cannot hold for one comparison with the same comparator class.
concerns: This candidate very likely dissolves on the comparator. The P-1364 summary block (summaries.md line ~191704) says serum CRP and IL-6 were significantly higher in NIC than in BOTH MCI and HC, 'reflecting the osteoarthritis control group'. The paper presents its NIC arm as proof that peripheral inflammatory markers are not AD-specific. So the 'lower in MCI' result compares MCI with an inflammatory-disease control group, not with healthy cognitively normal adults. On P-1364's own matching comparison (MCI vs healthy HC) the block reports no lower IL-6 in MCI: MCI 3.1 pg/mL is in the healthy range, and only the NIC value (42.8) is raised. The comparator population class therefore differs, and under H.1 that makes the comparison different. Further points: P-1377 P=0.013 is an omnibus three-group test (ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis across HC/MCI/AD), and the summary does not report a pairwise MCI-vs-HC post-hoc result. Both studies are small single-site cross-sectional samples (32 and 44 MCI) using different MCI criteria (NIA-AA biomarker-defined MCI due to AD vs Chinese clinical consensus). P-1248 (plasma IL-6 higher in MCI vs HC, India) agrees with P-1377 but uses plasma, not serum, so P-1377 is the closest counterpart. The CRP analog (P-1364 serum CRP lower in MCI vs NIC) was not proposed: its only opposite-direction counterpart, P-751, is in acute heart failure inpatients, a different population class, and the same osteoarthritis-comparator problem applies. The saliva cytokine atoms (P-1234) and the PD-MCI NLR atom (P-1369) were not proposed either: they differ in fluid and in population class. Recommend rejection at adjudication unless the full P-1364 text reports IL-6 lower in MCI than in its healthy HC arm.
source: summaries.md blocks Paper 1364 (line 191688) and Paper 1377 (line 192910)

quantity: Resting-state ALFF (P-513: ALFF/fALFF pooled) in the left superior temporal gyrus, from coordinate-based ALE meta-analysis
contrast: MCI vs healthy controls
finding_a: P-528 (ALE of 38 rs-fMRI studies, restricted to the dorsal attention network): MCI showed increased ALFF in the left and right STG (BA 39, 41). Cluster-level FWE p<0.05. Increased-ALFF pool: 321 subjects, 22 foci, 13 experiments.
finding_b: P-513 (ALE of 30 rs-fMRI studies, restricted to the salience network): MCI showed decreased ALFF/fALFF in the left STG (BA22), z=4.21, cluster-level FWE p<0.05. The same decrease appeared in the aMCI subset. Decreased-ALFF pool: 321 subjects across 12 experiments.
why_same_quantity: Both are ALE syntheses of published resting-state ALFF peak coordinates, both compare MCI with healthy controls, both come from pooled clinical MCI populations, and both name the left STG. The imaging index is the same (P-513 adds fALFF), and so are the contrast and the population class.
why_incompatible: Taken at the label level, the two meta-analyses report opposite significant convergent directions for ALFF in the left STG: an increase in P-528 and a decrease in P-513. Both survive FWE correction.
concerns: This is likely to dissolve when both papers are read. (1) The loci differ. P-513's cluster is lateral STG (BA22). P-528's is BA41 (transverse temporal/Heschl's gyrus) and BA39 (angular/posterior temporoparietal). They are distinct subregions that share only a gyrus label, so they may be different quantities. (2) ALE does not estimate a pooled effect with an interval. It maps spatial convergence of increase foci and decrease foci separately, so convergent increases and convergent decreases can both hold across the same literature. Neither result excludes the other the way opposite pooled estimates would. (3) The two analyses are companion network-restricted ALEs from the same group (SN vs DAN). Studies were selected per network, and seed and ROI choice was operator-dependent, which both papers acknowledge. The study pools probably overlap in part. (4) P-513 pools ALFF with fALFF, while P-528 is ALFF only. (5) P-528 reports left and right STG together.

quantity: Pooled standardised effect of exercise (any modality) vs control on overall cognition (cognitive outcomes pooled across domains) in older adults with MCI
contrast: exercise intervention vs non-exercise control, change from baseline to immediately post-intervention
finding_a: Standardised difference in means 1.165 (95% CI 0.741 to 1.589), Z=5.389, p<0.001; random effects over 20 effect entries from 23 controlled studies; I2=88%; prediction interval -0.747 to 3.077. Amnestic-MCI studies excluded from the cognitive pool. Composite cognitive scores combine all domains.
finding_b: Hedges' g 0.42 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.61), p<0.001; three-level random-effects model over 196 effect sizes from about 35 RCTs of exercise in MCI, pooled across nine cognitive domains; pre-post correlation imputed at 0.5.
why_same_quantity: Both are meta-analytic estimates of the same estimand: the effect of exercise of any modality against a non-exercise control on cognition pooled across domains, in clinically defined MCI in older adults. Both use a standardised mean difference (SMD vs Hedges' g, the same metric class) on change after the intervention. The P-680 block states that its cognitive pool combines all cognitive domains, and P-835 pools every domain in a multilevel model, so the outcome definitions correspond.
why_incompatible: This is not a disagreement about direction; both estimates favour exercise. The random-effects confidence intervals for the mean effect do not overlap (P-680 lower bound 0.741 > P-835 upper bound 0.61), and each interval excludes the other paper's point estimate. That meets only the rule's second limb ('estimates whose reported uncertainty excludes the other') and describes the same quantity at magnitudes that cannot both be true.
concerns: Weak at best. (1) Magnitude only: both papers conclude that exercise improves cognition in MCI, so no substantive claim is reversed. (2) Heterogeneity: P-680 has I2=88% and a prediction interval of -0.747 to 3.077, which contains 0.42. Once between-study heterogeneity is counted, the two estimates are compatible, and the non-overlap is only in CIs for the mean. (3) Design and pooling differ. P-680 admits controlled (Downs and Black-rated) studies, not RCTs only; it computes SDM from pre-post plus control data; it takes one composite per study and excludes amnestic MCI. P-835 is RCT-only, multilevel, uses change-score Hedges' g with an imputed r=0.5 and no sensitivity analysis, and has a very permissive MCI diagnostic gate. These method choices alone can plausibly produce a two- to threefold difference in SMD. (4) The included trials probably overlap substantially, so the gap is more likely a methods artefact than two independent bodies of evidence that disagree. (5) P-674 (SMD 0.65, 0.39 to 0.91) overlaps both, which suggests the literature is heterogeneous rather than contradictory. (6) Neither review has a risk-of-bias adjusted estimate (P-835 has no quality assessment; both show funnel asymmetry concerns). Recommend recording this as a magnitude discrepancy explained by pooling method and heterogeneity, not as a genuine contradiction, unless the operator reads the trial lists and finds largely non-overlapping evidence.

quantity: Adjusted association of female (vs male) sex with incident MCI in community-dwelling older adults who were cognitively intact at baseline
contrast: female vs male, incident MCI, covariate-adjusted, education adjusted in both (directly in P-646, through the cognitive-reserve composite in P-678)
finding_a: US HRS 1998-2018, adults 50+, Fine-Gray competing-risks model with death as the competing event, fully adjusted (including education and race): female SHR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88-1.03, p=0.27 (Table 2). The interaction models give SHR 0.98 (0.90-1.06). 4296 incident MCI cases over a mean 11.0 years; reported power 99.99%. MCI = Langa-Weir TICS-27 score of 7-11.
finding_b: CHARLS 2011/12 to 2015/16, adults 60+ intact at baseline (n=4420, 767 incident MCI), modified Poisson regression adjusted for age, marital status, smoking, drinking, comorbidity and the lifespan cognitive-reserve index: female vs male RR 1.88, 95% CI 1.59-2.23, p<0.001. MCI = CHARLS composite (TICS-10, word recall, figure drawing) more than 1 SD below age norms.
why_same_quantity: Both are population-level estimates of the effect of sex on developing MCI in general-population older adults with no MCI at baseline. Both adjust for education or an education proxy, and both come from harmonised HRS-family surveys (CHARLS was designed as a sister study of HRS). The rule admits different cohorts for a population-level association when both sample the same population class (community-dwelling older adults), so the dataset-family mismatch can be waived on that ground.
why_incompatible: The intervals exclude each other: P-646 is a precise, well-powered null (upper bound 1.03), and P-678's lower bound is 1.59. P-646's interval rules out any female excess of P-678's size, and P-678's rules out no association.
concerns: (1) Metric mismatch. P-646 reports a subdistribution HR (competing risk of death, about 11 years of follow-up). P-678 reports a risk ratio for one 3-4 year window. Both are risk ratios, and at 17% incidence the gap cannot be closed by converting, but the rule lists metric type as part of the estimand. (2) Different national populations (US vs China), ages 50+ vs 60+. Among older Chinese cohorts the female disadvantage in literacy is very large, and P-678's own block flags that its outcome tests are education-sensitive and normed on age only, not education. So the female RR may largely be measurement confounding, and the sex effect may genuinely differ between these populations rather than conflict. (3) MCI is operationalised differently: absolute TICS-27 cut-points vs below 1 SD on age norms, and neither is a clinical diagnosis. (4) Adjustment sets differ: P-646 adds race, depressive symptoms and behavioural covariates; P-678 adds a composite of education, occupation and leisure rather than education alone. (5) In both papers sex is a covariate, not the exposure of interest. Under the rule this is a precise null against a positive estimate, so moderate at best; with the metric and population caveats it is graded weak.
population_a: US Health and Retirement Study, community-dwelling adults aged 50+, 1998-2018
population_b: CHARLS, community-dwelling Chinese adults aged 60+ with intact cognition at baseline, 2011/12-2015/16
source: Atoms verified against summaries.md blocks P-646 (Table 2 SHR, interaction-model SHR, MCI definition, power) and P-678 (covariate RR, MCI definition, education-sensitivity caveat)

quantity: Crude (unadjusted) association of sex with prevalent MCI in community-dwelling older adults in East Asia
contrast: MCI vs cognitively normal, sex distribution (equivalently, MCI prevalence by sex), cross-sectional
finding_a: Toon Health Study, Japan, community-dwelling adults 60+ (n=1094, mean age 69.7): probable MCI (MoCA-J 25 or below) in 204/411 men (49.6%) vs 211/683 women (30.9%), P<0.01. Men are significantly more likely to have MCI.
finding_b: APFHCS, Tianjin/Shanghai, China, community-dwelling older adults (n=1367, mean age 71.0): women make up 71.8% of MCI cases vs 50.6% of the cognitively normal group, p<0.001. Women are significantly more likely to have MCI (MCI = education-specific MMSE cut-points plus IADL 6 or above).
why_same_quantity: Both report the same crude sex-MCI contrast (MCI vs normal cognition), which is mathematically equivalent whether expressed as prevalence by sex or sex distribution by group. Both are community-dwelling older adults of similar age (mean about 70-71) in general-population East Asian cohorts. This is a population-level association, not model performance, so the different-cohort pairing is admissible under the rule if the population class is accepted as the same.
why_incompatible: The directions are opposite and each is significant by the study's own test (men higher, P<0.01, vs women higher, p<0.001). They cannot both describe a single population's crude sex-MCI association.
concerns: (1) The crude sex-MCI prevalence association is not a transportable quantity. It is driven largely by country- and cohort-specific sex gradients in education and literacy, which are near-parity in older Japanese cohorts and strongly female-disadvantaged in older Chinese cohorts. The two results may each be true of their own populations, which makes this effect heterogeneity rather than a contradiction. (2) Different MCI instruments and education handling: MoCA-J at or below 25 with no education adjustment of the cut-point, vs MMSE education-specific cut-points plus IADL. Neither uses clinical adjudication. (3) Both are unadjusted: no age- or education-adjusted sex estimate is reported in either atom. (4) P-803's recruitment was invited geriatric assessment in two megacities, and P-822 drew on one prefecture's health-examination cohort. The male direction is also seen in P-825 (NCGG-SGS Japan, 70+, 50.3% vs 43.0% male, P=.002, normed NCGG-FAT battery) and the female direction in P-325 (CHARLS 2020, 45+, 15.3% vs 7.7%) and P-678 (CHARLS incident). The disagreement therefore tracks country, and P-822 vs P-803 was chosen as the most comparable pair (similar age, both screening-instrument MCI). Graded weak because the population-class equivalence is doubtful for a crude, education-confounded quantity.
population_a: Japanese community-dwelling adults aged 60+, Toon Health Study (Ehime)
population_b: Chinese community-dwelling older adults, APFHCS (Tianjin and Shanghai)
source: Atoms verified against summaries.md blocks P-822 (sex counts, MoCA-J cut-point, mean age) and P-803 (sex distribution, MMSE+IADL definition, mean age); corroborating blocks P-825, P-325 checked

quantity: ADAS-Cog change (points, lower = better) with manual/electro-acupuncture vs control in Chinese amnestic MCI, mean difference
contrast: acupuncture vs control arm, ADAS-Cog at end of treatment (P-760: 12 weeks vs untreated waitlist; P-759: pooled 4-8 week trials vs control)
finding_a: Single randomised, assessor-blinded, waitlist-controlled pilot RCT, n=40 (20/20): acupuncture -3.94 (-5.03 to -2.85) vs waitlist +1.72 (0.99 to 2.46); between-arm MD -5.66 (95% CI -6.98 to -4.35), which exceeds the stated 3-point MCID.
finding_b: Meta-analysis of 15 Chinese aMCI RCTs; the ADAS-Cog pool (2 trials, 72 participants, I2=0%) gives MD -1.00 (95% CI -1.23 to -0.77), p<0.00001, GRADE very low.
why_same_quantity: Same instrument (ADAS-Cog), same metric (mean difference in points), same population class (clinically diagnosed amnestic MCI in older Chinese adults), same intervention class (needle acupuncture) and the same kind of outcome (change vs a control arm at end of treatment). P-760 was published in 2025, after P-759's search closed (9 January 2024), so its trial is not one of the two pooled trials and the estimates are independent.
why_incompatible: Same direction, but the intervals do not overlap: P-760's upper bound (-4.35) is more than 3 points beyond P-759's lower bound (-1.23). Under the rule's 'uncertainty excludes the other' clause, both cannot be true of one acupuncture-vs-control ADAS-Cog effect. One says the effect is clinically important (over the MCID); the other says it is about a fifth of that.
concerns: This most likely fails on the comparator, which is one of the failure modes the rule names (a head-to-head trial against a network or mixed estimate vs control). P-760 compares against an untreated waitlist, and the waitlist arm got 1.72 points worse, about 30% of the net difference, plausibly nocebo or disengagement. P-759's controls across its 15 trials were donepezil (3), nimodipine (6), sham acupuncture (2), sham acupoint (2), rTMS (1) and waitlist (1), and at least three trials were add-on designs. The two ADAS-Cog trials cannot be identified from the block, so their comparators are unknown. P-759's own block says a difference against a waitlist and one against an active drug are not the same quantity. P-760's discussion states that sham-controlled trials found ADAS-Cog improvements that were significant but below the MCID. That is consistent with P-759's smaller estimate and explains the gap by comparator, not by a real clash. Other issues: P-759's ADAS-Cog pool is tiny (72 participants, fixed-effect, a CI implausibly narrow for n=72, very low GRADE certainty). P-760 is an unblinded-participant pilot with post-hoc power only and an ADAS-Cog baseline imbalance (11.85 vs 10.41, so regression to the mean favours acupuncture). Durations differ (12 weeks vs 4-8 weeks). Admissible only if the two pooled ADAS-Cog trials in P-759 turn out to be waitlist or no-treatment controlled. P-880 (VR+scalp/eye acupuncture vs VR alone, MoCA WMD 2.42 [1.98-3.06] vs P-759 MoCA 0.93 [0.80-1.07]) shows the same pattern of a large single-trial effect against a small P-759 pooled effect. It was not proposed separately because its contrast is an add-on over VR in general MCI.

quantity: Low muscle strength state (AWGS-type low grip / possible sarcopenia) and odds of MCI in community-dwelling Chinese older adults
contrast: low-strength state (possible sarcopenia present vs absent in P-878; low vs normal grip strength in P-682) vs normal strength, odds of MCI, fully adjusted logistic/GEE OR
finding_a: P-878 (CHARLS 2015, cross-sectional, adults 45+): possible sarcopenia OR 0.718 (95% CI 0.555-0.928, p=0.012), i.e. lower odds of prevalent MCI
finding_b: P-682 (SREHC rural Shandong, 60+, 3-wave GEE): low vs normal grip strength OR 1.78 (95% CI 1.51-2.10, p<0.001), i.e. higher odds of MCI
why_same_quantity: Under AWGS 2019 (the definition P-878 uses) possible sarcopenia is essentially the low-muscle-strength state (low handgrip, or low chair-stand/gait performance) without low muscle mass. P-682's exposure is low grip strength. Both are categorical low-strength exposures against a normal-strength reference, both use an OR for MCI with broad confounder adjustment, and both sample community-dwelling Chinese older adults. It is a population-level association, so the cohort difference (CHARLS vs SREHC) can be waived for that reason.
why_incompatible: The two directions are opposite and each is significant. P-878's interval (0.555-0.928) lies entirely below 1, and P-682's (1.51-2.10) lies entirely above it, so the intervals exclude each other. A low-strength state cannot both lower and raise the odds of MCI in the same population class.
concerns: Serious, and probably fatal on adjudication. (1) P-878's own table has an unresolved sign convention, and its block flags this. In the same fully adjusted table, handgrip per kg gives OR 1.047 (1.028-1.066), gait speed OR 1.571, FTSST OR 0.946, ASMI OR 1.405 and CESD score OR 0.956: every one points to better physical function or fewer depressive symptoms carrying HIGHER odds. Yet defined sarcopenia is OR 1.357 in the expected direction. That pattern fits the outcome, or the exposure codes, being reversed for most rows, so the possible-sarcopenia sign may be a reporting artefact rather than a finding. Check the paper's coding before admitting. (2) The exposures are not identical. Possible sarcopenia can be met by low physical performance alone, and P-878 treats defined sarcopenia as a separate category, so the reference group may differ from P-682's 'normal grip'. P-682's grip cut-off is not stated in the block. (3) The MCI definitions differ: P-878 uses the CHARLS telephone battery at 1 SD below the age norm (AACD), while P-682 uses education-stratified MMSE cut-offs. (4) The age bands differ (45+ vs 60+), as do the settings (national vs rural Shandong). (5) The designs differ: single-wave prevalent MCI in P-878 vs repeated-measures GEE across three waves in P-682. (6) P-878's direction also goes against the corpus: P-644 (Chinese community 60+, cross-sectional, handgrip OR 0.97 per kg), P-706, P-688 and P-733 all agree with P-682. P-878 therefore stands alone, and P-682 was chosen as its closest categorical comparator.
